name: ExifTool
purpose: Perl library and command-line tool that reads, writes and edits metadata in several hundred file formats, covering EXIF, IPTC, XMP, GPS, maker notes and embedded thumbnails.
journalism_use_case: First step on almost every image verification: dump the full metadata block to read capture time, GPS coordinates, device and lens, software history and embedded thumbnails. An embedded thumbnail that disagrees with the main image is a classic indicator that the visible picture was edited after capture.
pros: Unmatched format and maker-note coverage — it reads proprietary camera fields no other tool parses, which is often where the useful capture detail lives
The embedded-thumbnail extraction is a genuine forensic technique, not just metadata reading, and it has broken real cases
Entirely local with no dependencies beyond Perl, so it runs on an air-gapped evidence machine and nothing is transmitted
Exceptionally maintained for a single-maintainer project: release 13.64 and a near-empty tracker (19 open issues against 5,268 stars)
cons: Metadata is evidence about a file, not about reality: every field can be written or stripped — by ExifTool itself — so a plausible EXIF block is corroboration, never authentication
Most social platforms strip metadata on upload, so for the majority of circulating images there is simply nothing to read, and reporters misread that absence as suspicious
The output is dense and expert-oriented; a non-specialist will not know which of 400 fields matter
Perl dependency is unusual in a modern stack, and the write capability makes it easy to alter evidence accidentally if used carelessly
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,268 stars with only 19 open issues and a current tag (13.64), pushed 2026-11-16 — extraordinary maintenance consistency over two decades. ExifTool is the de facto standard underneath most other metadata tooling, verifiable from PyExifTool, Sherloq and ArchiveBox all depending on it.
assessment: Adopt unconditionally: it is the baseline instrument for image and document files and there is no substitute. For your profile two disciplines matter. First, work on copies — ExifTool can write, and an accidental write destroys the evidential value of the original. Second, train reporters that stripped metadata is the normal case for social media, so 'no EXIF' is not a finding. Pair with MediaInfo for video containers, where ExifTool is weaker.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest tag 13.64, no GitHub release objects (releases are published on exiftool.org), 5,268 stars, 19 open issues. Continuous releases over twenty years from a single maintainer with near-zero backlog — the strongest issue-throughput record in the catalogue.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 (the upstream distribution is also offered under the Artistic Licence — check the distribution you obtain). Embedding in a closed-source newsroom product would trigger copyleft; calling the CLI as a subprocess does not.
costs: No fee, no infrastructure, no paid dependencies. Among the cheapest high-value capabilities here.
privacy: Entirely local; nothing is transmitted, which makes it safe for source-sensitive material. The inverse risk matters more: ExifTool reveals GPS and device data in files you may intend to publish, so it is also the tool that tells you what to strip.
alternatives: PyExifTool to drive it from a Python pipeline
Exiv2 for a C++ library embedding path
MediaInfo for video container and encoder analysis
mat2 for removing rather than reading metadata
summary: Perl library and command-line tool that reads, writes and edits metadata in several hundred file formats, covering EXIF, IPTC…

name: PyExifTool
purpose: Python wrapper that runs ExifTool as a persistent subprocess and exposes its output as Python dictionaries, avoiding per-file process startup cost.
journalism_use_case: The practical way to metadata-profile a dump of thousands of images — clustering a leaked image set by camera body, software signature or capture-time gaps — inside a Python pipeline rather than by shelling out per file.
pros: Persistent-process design makes bulk metadata extraction fast enough for corpus-scale work, where naive per-file invocation would take hours
Returns structured dictionaries, so clustering by device or detecting timestamp anomalies becomes a few lines of pandas
Dual-licensed GPL-3.0-or-later OR BSD (user's choice), which is unusually flexible and removes the copyleft concern for a newsroom codebase
Thin wrapper, so it inherits ExifTool's full capability without reimplementing anything
cons: Inherits every interpretive caveat of ExifTool — metadata is editable and routinely stripped, so outputs support leads rather than conclusions
A wrapper, not a forensic method: it adds convenience, not analytical capability
Dormant: last push 2023-11-26 with release v0.5.6 (2023-10-22) and 28 open issues — three years without activity
Requires the ExifTool binary installed separately, so deployment has two moving parts and version skew between them is a real source of surprise
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 197 stars with 28 open issues, release v0.5.6 (2023-10-22), last push 2023-11-26, SPDX NOASSERTION with the dual GPL/BSD choice declared in the repository.
assessment: Still usable despite dormancy, because it is a thin wrapper around a tool that is itself impeccably maintained — the dependency-rot risk is low and the failure mode would be obvious. For your profile I would use it for bulk profiling work and pin both it and the ExifTool binary version in the pipeline. If it ever breaks, calling ExifTool with `-j` (JSON output) directly via subprocess is a half-hour replacement, which is worth knowing before you depend on it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2023-11-26, latest release v0.5.6 (2023-10-22), 197 stars, 28 open issues. Three years without commits. Mitigated by its nature: a thin wrapper over a stable CLI interface has very little surface to rot.
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later OR BSD (dual-licensed; user may choose) — GitHub reports NOASSERTION
licence_restrictions: The BSD option removes any copyleft concern for a newsroom codebase — choose it explicitly and record the choice.
costs: No fee. Requires the ExifTool binary. Negligible resources.
privacy: Local only; no network calls documented. Safe on an isolated machine.
alternatives: Calling `exiftool -j` directly via subprocess — a trivial and fully maintained substitute
Exiv2 bindings for a C++-backed library path
Apache Tika for metadata across a wider range of document formats
blockers: Dormant since 2023; have a direct-subprocess fallback in mind
summary: Python wrapper that runs ExifTool as a persistent subprocess and exposes its output as Python dictionaries…

name: Exiv2
purpose: C++ library and CLI for reading and writing image metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP and several maker-note dialects — with a stable API used by many desktop applications.
journalism_use_case: Embed metadata extraction into a newsroom ingest pipeline so every incoming image is automatically parsed for timestamps and GPS before an analyst sees it — the library route when you want metadata handling compiled into a service rather than shelling out to a Perl script.
pros: C++ library with a stable API makes it the right choice for embedding in a service, where ExifTool's subprocess model is awkward
Used by many desktop photo applications, so its parsing is exercised against a very wide range of real files
Actively maintained (v0.28.9, 2026-08-30; pushed 2026-11-16) with a long release history
GPL-2.0-or-later with a commercial licence also historically available — read the distribution you obtain
cons: Narrower maker-note coverage than ExifTool, so for forensic depth on camera-specific fields ExifTool remains better
Same fundamental caveat as all metadata tools: metadata is writer-controlled and routinely stripped, so it corroborates rather than proves
Engineer-facing with no analyst UI, and the C++ toolchain requirement makes it a heavier dependency than a Python wrapper
226 open issues, a substantial backlog reflecting the long tail of format edge cases
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 1,173 stars with 226 open issues, release v0.28.9 (2026-08-30), pushed 2026-11-16, SPDX NOASSERTION with GPL-2.0-or-later as the stated licence.
assessment: Choose it over ExifTool only when you need in-process metadata handling in a compiled service; otherwise ExifTool's coverage wins. For your profile that means Exiv2 is a build-time decision for a custom ingest service, not a tool you reach for interactively. If you are already running Apache Tika in the ingest path, its metadata output may make Exiv2 unnecessary.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.28.9 (2026-08-30), 1,173 stars, 226 open issues. Regular point releases on the 0.28 line with current commits from a community team.
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0-or-later: linking it into a closed-source product triggers copyleft. Historically a commercial licence has been available from the project — confirm current terms if you need one.
costs: No fee. C++ build toolchain; optional zlib/expat. Negligible runtime cost.
alternatives: ExifTool for maximum coverage via CLI
Apache Tika if you already run it for document metadata
PyExifTool for a Python-native path
summary: C++ library and CLI for reading and writing image metadata — EXIF, IPTC, XMP and several maker-note dialects…

name: MediaInfo
purpose: GUI and CLI tool reporting technical and tag information for video and audio files: container structure, codecs, bitrates, frame rates, encoder identification and writing-application fields.
journalism_use_case: Establish provenance signals on a submitted video before content analysis: which app or device wrote the file, whether the container layout matches a direct camera export or a WhatsApp/Telegram re-encode, and whether two 'different' files share an identical encoder fingerprint — which is how you spot that a 'new' video is a re-upload.
pros: Container and encoder fingerprinting answers the question reporters actually have about a video file — where has this been — which no content-analysis tool addresses
Identifies platform re-encodes, so you can tell a camera original from a WhatsApp forward, which determines whether any forensic analysis is even worth attempting
Fully local file inspection with no network dependency, appropriate for source-supplied material
Actively maintained (v26.10, 2026-10-06; pushed 2026-11-14) with both GUI and CLI, so analysts and pipelines are both served
cons: Reports only what the file declares: metadata is trivially stripped or forged, and almost every social platform re-encodes on upload, destroying original encoder fields — so absence of suspicious metadata means nothing
224 open issues, a large backlog for a tool of this scope
Interpreting container fingerprints requires experience; the raw report does not say 'this is a WhatsApp re-encode', you must know the signatures
Build-time GUI toolkit choice makes self-building awkward; most users take vendor packages
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 2,070 stars with 224 open issues, release v26.10 (2026-10-06), pushed 2026-11-14, BSD-2-Clause. MediaInfo is a standard tool in media and archiving workflows, reflected in its packaging across distributions.
assessment: Adopt as the mandatory first step on any submitted video, before anyone attempts forensic analysis — because it tells you whether the file is a camera original (worth analysing) or a platform re-encode (largely not). For your profile the high-value practice is building an internal reference of encoder fingerprints for the platforms and apps your region uses, so a reporter can be told 'this came through Telegram' rather than having to interpret the raw report.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v26.10 (2026-10-06), 2,070 stars, 224 open issues. Regular dated releases from a dedicated organisation (MediaArea) that also maintains MediaInfoLib and related tooling.
licence_restrictions: None material — permissive and safe to embed.
costs: No fee, no infrastructure. MediaArea offers paid support and custom development — optional, not required.
privacy: Entirely local file inspection with no network dependency.
alternatives: ExifTool for metadata on image and document files
ffprobe (FFmpeg) for a scriptable subset of the same container information
PySceneDetect for content-level rather than container-level video analysis
summary: GUI and CLI tool reporting technical and tag information for video and audio files: container structure, codecs, bitrates…

name: ImageHash
purpose: Python library implementing classic perceptual hashes — average, perceptual (DCT), difference, wavelet and colour hashes — for comparing images by visual similarity.
journalism_use_case: Build an in-house index of images you have already seen or debunked, then test whether a newly circulating image is a re-post, a crop or a lightly edited variant — the local alternative to pasting a sensitive image into a commercial reverse-image service, which would disclose it.
pros: Keeps reverse-image comparison entirely in-house, which is the decisive property when the image is source-supplied and must not be uploaded to Google or Yandex
Several hash algorithms with different robustness profiles, so you can compare and choose rather than trusting one
Tiny dependency surface (Pillow, NumPy, SciPy) and simple enough to audit fully
Large user base (3,887 stars) with a modest backlog (29 open issues)
cons: A hash match is a probabilistic similarity signal, not provenance and not proof — it says two files look alike, not which came first or whether either is authentic
Classic perceptual hashes degrade under cropping, overlays, heavy recompression and rotation, which is exactly what happens to images in circulation — PDQ is more robust
Release metadata is confusing: the GitHub release object is v4.1.0 (2021-03-25) while the current tag is v4.3.2, so pinning requires care
No index or storage layer — you build the matching infrastructure around it
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 3,887 stars with 29 open issues, release object v4.1.0 (2021-03-25) against tag v4.3.2, last push 2026-10-12. The release/tag divergence is visible in the API and is a genuine pinning annoyance.
assessment: Adopt for the in-house image index — the privacy argument makes it clearly preferable to commercial reverse search for unpublished material. For your profile I would use PDQ (from ThreatExchange) as the primary hash because of its robustness to crops and overlays, and keep ImageHash for its algorithm variety and simplicity. Store hashes with the provenance of each image, since the index's value is knowing where you saw something first.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-12, release object v4.1.0 (2021-03-25), latest tag v4.3.2, 3,887 stars, 29 open issues. Commits within the last month but release engineering has lapsed; a mature library at low velocity.
costs: No fee. CPU only; negligible. Storage for the hash index is trivial relative to the images.
privacy: Local only; no external service required. The index itself is a record of what your newsroom has examined, so protect it accordingly.
alternatives: ThreatExchange PDQ for crop- and overlay-robust hashing at scale
imagededup for corpus deduplication with CNN embeddings as an option
blockhash-python where a documented interoperable algorithm matters more than accuracy
summary: Python library implementing classic perceptual hashes — average, perceptual (DCT), difference, wavelet and colour hashes…

name: ThreatExchange (PDQ / TMK+PDQF / vPDQ and HMA)
purpose: Collection of production perceptual-hashing algorithms (PDQ for images, TMK+PDQF and vPDQ for video) plus Hasher-Matcher-Actioner, a deployable service for hashing and matching media against hash banks.
journalism_use_case: Industry-standard hashing for a collaborative or newsroom-scale image and video corpus: hash incoming media and match against a bank of previously verified or previously debunked content, including across organisations. TMK+PDQF in particular makes video-level matching practical, which is how you trace a clip's spread across platforms.
pros: PDQ is materially more robust than classic perceptual hashes to cropping, overlays and recompression — the transformations media actually undergoes in circulation
Video hashing (TMK+PDQF, vPDQ) addresses a real gap: almost nothing else open lets you match video at scale
Hasher-Matcher-Actioner provides a deployable service rather than just algorithms, with releases (hma-v1.2.2, 2026-11-04) and active development
BSD-3-Clause on the repository, so the algorithms are freely usable — note the pdq/cpp/CImg.h and tmk/LICENSE.txt sub-licences called out in the README
cons: These are near-duplicate matching tools, NOT manipulation or AI-generation detectors: a match means 'substantially the same media as something in the bank' and says nothing about authenticity — a distinction that is persistently misunderstood
Video hashing degrades under re-encoding and editing, so matching across platform re-uploads is imperfect
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION because of the mixed sub-licences, so a compliance review needs the per-directory detail rather than a single label
HMA deployment implies container or cloud infrastructure; connecting a signal-exchange API means exchanging hashes with a third party under partner terms
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,411 stars with 58 open issues, release hma-v1.2.2 (2026-11-04), pushed 2026-11-09; the repository transfer facebook/ThreatExchange → meta/ThreatExchange was confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17. PDQ is widely used in industry content-matching, which is the relevant production context.
assessment: The right hashing foundation for a newsroom that handles media at volume or collaborates across organisations — PDQ for images, vPDQ for video, and HMA only if the volume justifies a service. For your profile the critical governance point is bank hygiene: a hash bank of 'previously debunked' content is an editorial asset that must be curated, because an incorrect entry silently mislabels future media. Keep hashing local and treat any hash exchange with a platform as a separate decision with its own terms.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release hma-v1.2.2 (2026-11-04), SPDX NOASSERTION (BSD-3-Clause repository licence with separate sub-licences), 1,411 stars, 58 open issues. Current releases under corporate maintenance; transfer from the facebook org confirmed.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (repository LICENSE; README notes pdq/cpp/CImg.h carries its own separate licence and tmk/LICENSE.txt is BSD-2-Clause) — GitHub reports NOASSERTION
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Hash banks you obtain from partners carry their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Mixed sub-licences mean a per-directory review is needed before redistribution. The CImg dependency in the C++ PDQ implementation is the specific item to check, since CImg's own licence is not BSD.
costs: No fee. FFmpeg 4.1+ recommended for video hashing; optional OpenMP and FAISS. HMA implies container or cloud infrastructure — a small service for newsroom volumes. Estimate.
privacy: Hashing and local matching need no network. Connecting an exchange API sends and receives hashes (not images) with a third party under partner terms — a deliberate decision, and note that a hash still reveals that you hold a matching image.
alternatives: ImageHash for simpler local image hashing
imagededup for corpus-scale deduplication
pHash where audio or video fingerprinting with a different algorithm is wanted
summary: Collection of production perceptual-hashing algorithms (PDQ for images, TMK+PDQF and vPDQ for video) plus…

name: imagededup
purpose: Python library for finding duplicate and near-duplicate images using either perceptual hashing or CNN embeddings, with evaluation tooling for threshold selection.
journalism_use_case: Deduplicate a large scraped image corpus before manual review, collapsing thousands of reposts into unique images so analyst time goes to genuinely new material — the image equivalent of datasketch's role in document triage.
pros: Offers both hashing and CNN-embedding methods with evaluation tooling, so you can measure the trade-off on your own corpus rather than guessing a threshold
Solves the actual bottleneck in image-corpus work, which is analyst attention rather than compute
Apache-2.0 with reasonable documentation and a substantial user base (5,686 stars)
Threshold evaluation support is unusual and genuinely useful — most dedup tools leave you to guess
cons: Duplicate groupings are similarity judgements requiring a tuned threshold; an untuned run will either merge distinct images or miss obvious reposts
CNN embeddings cluster semantically similar but distinct images — two different protests look alike to the model — which is wrong for forensic identity and is the most common misuse
Development has slowed: release v0.3.3.post2 and last push both 2025-08-15, fifteen months before this survey
Deep-learning runtime needed for the CNN method, which is a heavy dependency for what is otherwise a simple library
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 5,686 stars with 39 open issues, release v0.3.3.post2 (2025-08-15) with the last push the same day — a project that stopped cleanly at a release rather than drifting. The semantic-clustering behaviour of CNN embeddings is a documented property of the method, not a defect.
assessment: Use the hashing method for forensic identity and avoid the CNN method for that purpose — use CNN embeddings only when you deliberately want semantic grouping (for example 'show me all the protest photos'). For your profile the dormancy is tolerable because the hashing path has essentially no dependency rot risk, but if you need the CNN path I would build it on sentence-transformers-style embeddings you control instead, so the model choice is explicit.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-08-15, latest release v0.3.3.post2 published the same day, 5,686 stars, 39 open issues. Fifteen months with no activity following a release; a corporate open-source project that appears to have been set aside. Declining rather than dormant given the clean final release.
model_or_data_licence: CNN method uses pretrained weights fetched on first use; their licences were not individually verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Verify the CNN backbone's weights licence if you use that method commercially.
costs: No fee. CPU sufficient for hashing; GPU optional and only helpful for CNN embeddings. Model weights fetched once. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing; model weights fetched once from a third-party host. Images are not uploaded.
alternatives: ImageHash plus your own index for a simpler, maintained hashing path
ThreatExchange PDQ for more robust hashing at scale
Bellingcat smart-image-sorter where semantic grouping is actually what you want
summary: Python library for finding duplicate and near-duplicate images using either perceptual hashing or CNN embeddings…

name: pHash
purpose: C++ library implementing perceptual hashes for images, audio and video, with DCT, radial and marr-hildreth image hashes plus audio and video fingerprinting.
journalism_use_case: Match a short audio or video clip against a reference library to identify re-used broadcast or propaganda material, where image-only hashing is insufficient — for instance recognising that a 'new' leaked recording is a segment of a years-old broadcast.
pros: Audio fingerprinting is the distinguishing capability and a real gap elsewhere in this catalogue: almost nothing open lets you match audio clips against a reference library
Multiple image hash algorithms including radial and marr-hildreth, which behave differently under rotation and blur than DCT hashes
Still receiving commits (pushed 2026-06-09) with an essentially empty issue tracker (2 open)
Long-established algorithms with published descriptions, so the method is citable in a methodology note
cons: GPL-3.0 copyleft constrains embedding in closed newsroom products — a real consideration if you build a service around it
Low-level library with sparse modern documentation; audio and video hashing need careful parameterisation and there is little guidance
Matches are similarity signals only, and audio fingerprinting degrades with heavy compression or background noise
No releases at all and a C++ toolchain with CImg and FFmpeg dependencies, so building it is a project
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 664 stars with 2 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-06-09, GPL-3.0. The near-empty tracker on a library of this age more likely reflects low use than perfect quality.
assessment: Worth the build effort only if audio matching is a specific need — and for monitoring broadcast or propaganda reuse, it genuinely is. For your profile I would scope it narrowly: build a reference library of the broadcasts and recordings relevant to one investigation, fingerprint incoming clips against it, and treat matches as leads. For image work, PDQ and ImageHash are better supported and easier.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-09, no releases or tags, 664 stars, 2 open issues. Five months since last push on a long-established library with minimal churn; stable rather than declining, though documentation and release engineering are effectively absent.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 copyleft: embedding in a closed-source newsroom product triggers source obligations. Internal use and CLI invocation are unaffected.
costs: No fee. C++ toolchain, CImg, FFmpeg for video/audio. Build effort is the real cost; no paid dependencies.
privacy: Entirely local, no network, no models.
alternatives: ThreatExchange vPDQ/TMK+PDQF for video matching with better support
Chromaprint/AcoustID for audio fingerprinting with a maintained ecosystem
ImageHash for the image-only case
summary: C++ library implementing perceptual hashes for images, audio and video, with DCT…

name: blockhash-python
purpose: Python implementation of the blockhash perceptual-hashing algorithm, which divides an image into blocks and derives a hash from block median values.
journalism_use_case: A simple, dependency-light hash for deduplicating image sets where a documented, interoperable algorithm matters more than peak accuracy — for example when two organisations need to compare hashes and must agree on the exact algorithm.
pros: The algorithm is simply and publicly specified, so hashes are reproducible across independent implementations — useful for cross-organisation comparison where PDQ's complexity is a barrier
Minimal dependencies (Pillow only) and short enough to read in full, which makes it auditable
MIT licensed with no restrictions at all
cons: Dormant: last push 2023-10-31, no releases, 131 stars — three years without activity
Superseded in practice by ImageHash and PDQ; blockhash is less robust than PDQ to cropping and overlays, which is the condition that matters
Similarity signal only, with all the usual caveats about hashes proving nothing about authenticity
Tiny community means no support and no ecosystem
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 131 stars with 4 open issues, no releases, last push 2023-10-31, MIT licence.
assessment: Hard to justify today: ImageHash covers the same ground with more algorithms and active maintenance, and PDQ is better where robustness matters. The one scenario where blockhash earns its place is cross-organisation interoperability with a partner who has already implemented it — the specification's simplicity is its only remaining advantage. For your profile I would default to PDQ and ImageHash.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2023-10-31, no releases or tags, 131 stars, 4 open issues. Three years without activity. Low practical risk given the trivial dependency surface, but no reason to choose it.
alternatives: ImageHash — recommended: more algorithms, maintained
ThreatExchange PDQ for robustness to crops and overlays
imagededup for corpus-scale deduplication
blockers: Dormant since 2023 and superseded by better-maintained alternatives
summary: Python implementation of the blockhash perceptual-hashing algorithm, which divides an image into blocks and derives a hash from…
